region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II: Dierstories (1920), No. 26

summary.en: The Crow finds a sick springbok he cannot kill; he begs help from vulture, lion, wolf, jackal and baboon in turn, quarrelling with each under his boast 'My name is Hunter Straightshot' — until only the snake, bought with a mouse, can bite the buck; and lion, jackal and wolf eat everything while he screams 'It is my buck I shot!'
summary.zh: 鴉遇病羚而不能殺；求兀鷲、獅、狼、豺、狒狒——皆因自詡「吾名直射獵手」而起爭執——終以鼠換蛇噬羚；而獅豺狼食盡其獲，他唯呼「此吾所射之羚！」

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 26 (1920); not verbatim. The Crow felt hungry and saw a sick springbok lying under a bush; but he saw no chance to kill the sick animal, and tried to peck out its eyes — yet the springbok was not so sick, and butted the Crow away with its horns every time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He went for help, but quarrelled with the Vulture ('why are you so dirty?'), the Lion ('your eyes sit behind on the heels of your feet'), the Wolf ('you carry your eyes in your belly'), the Jackal ('you eat so much gum your eyelashes are glued together') and the Baboon, until he caught a mouse and bought the Snake's help with it; but the snake swallowed the mouse and lay still for a long time digesting.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. By the time the Crow came back the buck was too weak to fight; he picked out the eyes and tongue while it still lived. The Lion smelled the blood and came and ate; the Jackal gnawed the sinews; the Wolf gnawed the bones; and each time the Crow screamed from the tree: 'Who is there? Let go: it is my springbok that I shot for myself!' The Lion answered: 'If you had not been so insolent with me, I would have left you something; but now nothing!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 26; not verbatim.

title.en: The Vultures: The Lover Who Became a Bird

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 27

summary.en: A young Bushman madly in love changes into a vulture to fly over the mountains to his girl; that very night lions fall on her parents' huts and eat everyone but the three sisters sleeping in the walled-up rock cave. He opens it, changes all three into vultures, marries her — and the greedy cliff-vultures strip every kill his household makes, so they must fly away and live with the vultures who hunt together.
summary.zh: 少年戀人化兀鷲飛山赴其愛人；當夜獅群襲其父母之屋，食盡眾人，唯三姐妹於封石之穴得免。他啟穴，化三人皆為兀鷲，娶之——而貪婪之崖鷲食盡其獵獲，遂不得不飛離，與群獵之兀鷲同居。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 27 (1920); not verbatim. A young Bushman was madly in love with a young Bushman girl; but her father and his had constant quarrels, and her father moved away beyond the mountains. Every night the young man dreamed he could fly over the mountains to where the girl's parents lived, and woke with a sore heart; until one day he managed to change himself into a vulture, for he was one of the Bushmen of the old race.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 27; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He flew over the mountains, found the place, and sat near her; when she raised a stone to throw he changed himself into a Bushman. He meant to change her into a vulture too, so that their parents could not know them; but that night lions attacked the huts and ate all that slept there — only the three girls in the little rock cave, which the parents walled up every night, survived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 27; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. In the morning he flew over the huts, saw what had happened, opened the rock-house for the three sisters, changed them into vultures — for they also belonged to the old race — took the girl for his wife, and they flew to the mountains to live with the other cliff-vultures, who were also Bushmen of the old race. But the other cliff-vultures grew lazy and ate up every kill; so at last the man and his wife flew away to live with vultures who seek food together.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 27; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 28

summary.en: The toothless, day-shy aardvark marries a warthog woman and orders her to empty her kaross of its back-skin for his ants' eggs; she refuses thrice, he tears the skin half off her back, and the zebra beats him off. Since then warthogs and zebras graze together, the aardvark wanders solitary by night, and no bush-pig girl will have him.
summary.zh: 無齒畏晝之土豚娶疣豬女，命她脫背皮以盛蟻卵；三拒之，他撕其背皮半幅，斑馬擊退之。自兹疣豬與斑馬同牧；土豚夜行孤獨，林豬之女無一肯嫁。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 28 (1920); not verbatim. Aardvark took a wife from the warthogs. He has no front teeth and is ashamed, fearing the others will mock him; so he seeks his food by night. His wife, Warthog, seeks hers by day and at first would not marry him: 'I work in the day, but by night I want to sleep.' He answered: 'In the day I will not walk about, for they laugh at my big ears and mock me because I have no teeth; but come with me, and I shall teach you to see well by night, for we both belong to the old race.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 28; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When his knapsack was full of Bushman-rice he ordered her to bring her back-kaross to pour the rice on; three times she refused — 'we warthogs never walk without our back-skin kaross; bury the rice in the ground.' Then Aardvark flew at her and tore the skin half off her back with his great claws, and her entrails came out; she wept, and the zebra fought, kicked and drove him away. Her mother fetched her home sick.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 28; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. From then on the warthogs and the zebras graze together. Aardvark repented his attack on his wife, wandered about helpless, and tried to take a bush-pig girl for a wife; but because they can see well by night and know what he did, they would not have him and all mocked him, so that the aardvark wanders to this day as a solitary wanderer by night, still gathering Bushman-rice — but they took his knapsack away, and now he must eat everything he digs up.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 28; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 29

summary.en: The lazy dancing Hare teases the little Tingtinkie all night, shaking his nest until the bird bolts in the dark; then he confesses it was the Owl all along. The birds torment the Owl by day — though the truth is that Hare was the boy who strove with the Moon; Tingtinkie stayed child-size from eating forbidden fruit; and the Owl was a sorcerer whose power was broken, but who still knows what will happen within a month.
summary.zh: 懶舞之兔徹夜捉弄亭亭雀，搖其巢令其黑暗中亂撞；後自認乃梟所為。眾鳥晝擾梟——其實兔即昔日與月相爭之少年；亭亭雀因食禁果而不長；梟本巫者，法力被奪，然仍知一月內將發生之事。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 29 (1920); not verbatim. Hare was always a fellow who looked out for showing off; of hunting he never was fond, but dancing was his vocation: he rattled about the whole night, and by day, when one must hunt, he slept his body out... Because he was too lazy to fetch water, the dew and the sap of juicy plants were enough to quench his thirst.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 29; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. That Hare now lives so withdrawn he himself is to blame; for earlier he was the swaggering fellow who dared to strive with the Moon and to contradict her that all would come alive again after they had died a while; for this they hated him, and even his wife and children do not live with him. Tingtinkie was in his childhood disobedient and ate of the veld-fruits his parents had forbidden; the poison in those fruits made that he grew no more, so he kept the size of a child, however old he became.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 29; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Night after night Hare shook Tingtinkie's hanging nest, till the bird got the convulsions of all the fright; then Hare said with a laugh that it was not he but the Owl who had frightened him. Tingtinkie told all the birds that it was the Owl with his great eyes who chased death onto their bodies by night; the birds believed it, left Hare, and plagued and teased the Owl in the day. The Owl was an old sorcerer, but a greater and mightier sorcerer broke his power and took it from him — yet to tell things beforehand they could not take from him: the Owl still knows what goes on far away and what will happen within a month.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 29; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bushman and the Lion Meet in a Cave

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 30

summary.en: The lion makes rain so dark that a lost Bushman creeps into the very cave where the lion waits; feeling the hairy ribs, he tiptoes out, swims the torrent the lion's own rain has raised, takes the lion's glowing eyes for a fire, hides in a rock-slit that opens on a second chamber where two armed Bushmen sleep, and the three keep the fire till dawn — for the lion fears burning brands more than assegais.
summary.zh: 獅降雨蔽天，迷途桑人誤入獅候之穴；觸其毛肋，踮足而出，泅渡獅雨所漲之洪，誤認獅目為火光，匿入石縫——縫通暗室，內有二持弓桑人。三人守火至旦：獅畏燃柴甚於矛。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 30 (1920); not verbatim. The Lion got a plan one evening, when the sun went down, to make rain; he let the sky grow so dark that one could not see one's hands before one's eyes, and it rained as if old maids and knobkerries were falling out of the sky together. One Bushman quite lost his way; he knew he was near a cave, but where exactly it was he could not say.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 30; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Lion noticed the Bushman seeking the cave, ran ahead in the rain and cold, and curled up waiting inside. The Bushman crept in feeling his way, heard someone breathing hard — too hard for a man — and laid his hand softly on a hairy something: it was none other than the Lion, a perfect giant! Softly as a cat he crept back and tiptoed out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 30; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He knew the lion would get his scent and follow, so he swam a stream — for the lion is a little averse to running water, which its own rain had filled. In the dark he saw a fire glowing and thought it was the lion's eye; a rock-slit received him, and it opened on another chamber where two lost Bushmen slept by a fine fire, bows and arrows ready. 'Push out that man who dared to plague me in my house!' roared the lion; 'Come and fetch him out yourself if you are man enough,' they answered — and they kept up the fire till daylight, when the lion slunk away, for he will not attack men in clear daylight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 30; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 31

summary.en: Two old Bushmen each have a son: the good one, whose arms and legs a jealous father cuts off, becomes the great field tortoise; the second, beheaded by the sorcerer father of the first, is split lengthwise — and when the Jackal comes to eat the pieces, the Moon drops her dew on them and each piece stretches into a long field snake. Snake and Tortoise never quarrel to this day.
summary.zh: 兩老桑人各有一子：善者被妒父斷其四肢，化為大草原龜；次子被首者被縱剖為二——豺來食之，月滴露其上，每片伸長為長蛇。蛇與龜至今不相爭。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 31 (1920); not verbatim. There were two old Bushmen of the old race; each had a son. But the son of the one was a good-for-nothing, and the son of the other was clever at hunting, and could dance beautifully and play the ramkie; this made jealousy between the two fathers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. One day the father of the good-for-nothing caught the good son alone in the veld; he took him by treachery, cut off his arms and legs, took his beautiful knitted kaross and gave him a piece of hard old buffalo hide in exchange. The good son, with neither arms nor legs to hunt, dance or make music, crawled about and became the great field tortoise.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The sorcerer father next bewitched his own stout son into a gorgeous bird, waited till the tortoise's young brother crept near, sprang down as an old Bushman, cut off the boy's head and split him from below upwards into two pieces, each with an arm and leg. When the sun went down and the moon came out, the Jackal came to eat the pieces; but the Moon, who comes alive again month after month, poured her dew on the two pieces, the arm and leg of each stretched out, and each piece became a long field snake. The father found the great field snakes but did not know them; and Tortoise knew they were his brothers, so Snake and Tortoise never quarrel to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 31; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 32

summary.en: At a zebra kill the lioness scatters the pack while cubs bellow; Wolf whimpers 'how-hoo' and Jackal laughs 'ha-ga-ga!' with a dry tongue; when they circle back for scraps the lion slides in beneath them and rakes them both. Wolf learns to eat at the meat, Jackal to beg with one eye on the vulture and one on Wolf — because they too were once Bushmen.
summary.zh: 斑馬獲處，母獅驅散獸群，幼獅怒吼；狼泣「霍霍」，豺乾舌而笑「哈嘎嘎」；二人回頭覓食，獅潛其下抓傷二獸。狼學得就肉而食，豺學得一日視鷲、一日視狼而乞——因彼等本亦是桑人。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 32 (1920); not verbatim. Lion also belongs to the old race; therefore he is Lion. His hunting mates walk about little. Wolf can also hunt... but where Lion still stands and says 'Dare to come near!', Wolf has long since thrown down the reins and run till he grew small. Of Jackal there is nothing to say! He is a beggar, bolts at the smallest rustle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. When the sun went down Lion stood up, sniffed against the wind: 'Aha, wife, I smell zebras — they are here near; come with the children behind me as soon as I have the zebra down.' The lioness rounded the zebras, her mate sprang, held the prey with teeth behind the neck... The two eldest cubs tore strips from the skin to make eating-places for the little ones.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf and Jackal drew near at the smell of blood. 'Please, Lion, give me also a piece,' begged Wolf; 'and me too,' begged Jackal. 'Wau! Haau!' was all Lion said, as he tried how deep he could drive his claws into Wolf's hide; Wolf wept and fled... but when they saw the lioness eating again, they came foot for foot nearer — until Lion slid in unawares under the two quarrel-makers: Jackal got a few scratches and Wolf enough to make his hair fly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf then saw it paid him better to look after his body at the meat and marrowbones than to keep Jackal from it; and Jackal knows it does not become him to eat too near Wolf: he sits, head in the air, tongue out, crying out his heart in sorrow — one eye on the meat, the other on Wolf. That they are so clever is because they too were once Bushmen, who have now become Lion, Wolf and Jackal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 32; not verbatim.

title.en: The Baboons, the Apes and Little Jantjie

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 33

summary.en: Jantjie, a Bushman child taken by white hunters, runs away stuffed with stolen flour and tobacco; the apes — old Korannas — and the baboons — old Bushmen — want his bundle, and the children cry 'kill him and give us the nice grains'. At the river he bangs his tin pail like a thousand-pound cannon and the apes bolt; in the rocks he cannot, so he mocks their flat overhanging foreheads, cries 'Boer, bring your gun!' and escapes over the kranses.
summary.zh: 小揚奇為白獵者所擄之桑童，攜競得之粉與煙逃亡；猿（古科蘭人）與狒狒（古桑人）欲奪其包，幼者呼「殺之予我香粒！」。河邊他敲錫桶如千磅巨炮，猿群奔逃；岩間不能敲，遂譏其平懸之額，呼「布爾人，帶槍來！」，越崖而遁。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; colonial-era setting; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 33 (1920); not verbatim. Hunters from the sunset side (from the sea side) once came and caught a Bushman child and took it home with them; the hunters were white people, and they named the little Bushman Jantjie... He made a plan to run away, and days beforehand packed food quietly in his knapsack: bread, meal, wheat, meat, fish and whatever he could get hold of sneakily — especially tinderboxes and firesteels, knives and tobacco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The land he had to flee through was inhabited by apes and baboons. The apes lived along a great river and were said to be old Korannas that became apes; and the baboons farmed in the ridge-country and were said to be old Bushmen changed into baboons, now living on veld-food and insects. At the river the apes said: 'Let us go for the man: he carries goods; let us kill him and take the goods.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Jantjie got the thought that apes fear a great noise. He mocked them — 'why are your bottoms so black? just above your eyes the skin is still white if you roll your eyes back' — till they stormed him; then he banged on the tin pail and made a thousand-pounder noise; the apes were frightened and flew off, the children wailed, the old ones roared from above and fled into the high trees. At the baboons' rocks the pail was full of water and useless, so he mocked their foreheads — 'like a krans at the front of a ridge' — and cried: 'Boer, boer, bring your gun! Here are the ugly ones you seek!' and while they fled to the cliffs he made off home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 33; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 34

summary.en: A father shoots a lion that carried off his baby; later a water-spirit pulls his daughter into a pool and the mother fights her way out with her. Years on, the two children are lost in the veld; the father and sons seek by day, the mother and daughters by night, calling, until worn to skin and bone they become the sunbeetles (doringbesies) that sing and seek by day, and the crickets that sing and seek by night.
summary.zh: 父射殺奪嬰之獅；後水靈曳其女入池，母搏鬥救出。多年後二子失於原野；父與子晝尋、母與女夜尋，呼號不輟，直至形銷骨立——化為晝歌晝尋之日甲蟲，與夜歌夜尋之蟋蟀。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 34 (1920); not verbatim. An old Bushman and his wife had one little boy; they went to dig Bushman-rice, and the child fell asleep on the mother's back-kaross under a bush. A lion that had eaten its fill at a hartebeest picked up the kaross with the child and lay down near by to watch what the parents would do. The father climbed a bobbejaan-tou, shot the lion with his last poisoned arrow in the open throat, and brought home meat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Years passed; a girl child came, and when she could play about, the mother was cutting matjiesgoed by the fountain. The child picked reeds too near the pool; the water-spirit came out and drew the child in; the mother leapt into the water, wrestled with the water-spirit at great risk of her life, saved her child and swam out, exhausted and half dead.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The father played the violin and the mother the ramkie beautifully, and the two children danced before them; they spent many a pleasant evening and night by the veld-fire. One day the two children were sent for veld-food and never came back: the parents sought and called and played violin and ramkie, but no answer came; the father asked the Hammerkop, who sees all in the water, and the mother the Owl, whose dolosse stood still. So father and sons seek by day, mother and daughters by night — and worn out with grief they became the sunbeetles and the crickets, the one singing and seeking by day, the other by night.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 34; not verbatim.

title.en: Lion and Wolf Eat Over and Over

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 35

summary.en: The stingy Lion palms off two sucked marrowbones on the begging Wolf; Wolf invites him to ostrich soup, pretends to feed wife and children from a cold pot, then pours the boiling one over the lion's head and claps it tight — and brains him with his kierie. So a mean deed always comes back on a man's own head.
summary.zh: 吝獅以兩根吮盡之髓骨欺乞食之狼；狼邀其飲鴕湯，假作以冷釜飼妻兒，實傾沸釜於獅首而扣緊——復以短杖擊斃之。故刻薄之行，終返其人之首。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; graphic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 35 (1920); not verbatim. Wolf was out the whole night on the hunt without luck; near daybreak he came on Lion's spoor and followed it, for he knows Lion is a lucky fellow who always gets food. Lion had caught a zebra and eaten his fill... 'And there lies more than half a zebra still,' noted Wolf. 'Yes, but that I must keep for my wife and children,' said Lion, and went and fetched a marrowbone whose marrow he had sucked out himself: 'There, eat.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Wolf took the bone, gave it a few licks, and asked to be allowed to lick the sops by the zebra; Lion said he himself was so fond of soup he would not give away a drop. Wolf asked for a bone to take home, and got another cleaned-out one: 'There, take it; you beggar. Now go!'... 'Now I ask you, brother Lion, to come and eat at my place to-morrow.' On the way home Wolf caught an ostrich and ate his fill of it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Next day he cooked the ostrich flesh, poured the cold soup into another pot, and kept the fresh one boiling; when Lion came he pretended to feed his wife and children soup by the mouthful — then set the empty pot down and took up the boiling one: 'Now it is our turn; we have time and can drink at our ease — you first, then I.' He turned the pot of boiling soup over Lion's head and pressed the hot pot fast over it; Lion's eyes, mouth and throat were scalded; he dropped to the ground, and Wolf took his kierie and battered him dead. So a mean deed always comes back on a man's own head.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 35; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 36

summary.en: The hunter Raakskiet is trampled senseless by a bewitched ostrich; thirsting for water, he crawls to the pool and drowns. His family find him, lay him in the sun, and kill the boy's pet hare 'for the hare brought death into the world'. As they mourn, Raakskiet revives in the sun. Later a whirlwind carries one bloody plume into the pool where he drowned, and it becomes a little ostrich that grows and returns to his wives.
summary.zh: 獵者直射者遭妖鴕踏暈；渴極爬至池邊而溺斃。家人置屍日下曝之，並殺其子之寵兔「因兔帶死亡入世」。眾方哀哭，直射者日下復甦。後旋風捲一血羽入其溺斃之池，化為小鴕，漸長而歸其妻。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 36 (1920); not verbatim. Raakskiet (Straightshot) was known as one of the best hunters of his time... He felt sick and decided to turn back home; an ostrich cock came behind him, blew mightily and wanted only to kick and trample him. He lay flat; the bird sat on him with its sharp breastbone and kneaded him as if it would press him flat like a foot-sole; the string of his bow broke under the kicks.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He bound himself over with twigs so that he looked like a bush and so escaped home, took to his bed, and lay sick. Thirsting for water he crawled to the pool and fell forward into the water and was drowned. The family found him in the water dead, rolled him on the ground, and laid him in the sunshine by the pool to get warm; and the mother killed the boy's pet hare, for the hare is food with which one may not play, and death came into the world through a hare.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. But just then his father Raakskiet came alive again; he raised himself, sat in the sunshine, grew better with every breath, and stood up lacking nothing. Later a mighty whirlwind came and whirled all the plumes away; one feather heavy with blood could not whirl so high, came down, and fell into the pool in which Raakskiet had drowned the day before, and swam on the water: while they watched, that bloody feather changed into a little ostrich. The little creature took its down-feathers; they grew; it stepped with weak legs out of the water, sat basking in the sun, grew stronger and stronger — and an adult bird, black and white, trotted off straight to its own home to tell its wives it still lived.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 36; not verbatim.

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1920

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel II (1920), No. 37

summary.en: The lionesses praise Ape's springing, Gemsbok's speed and Ostrich's booming; the jealous lions stage a feast, scratch ape's rump, score gemsbok's face, strip ostrich's rump feathers, and stalk off — but hunt ostriches for their lungs till they boom from the chest. The wives learn the value of their providers; and one wife's mockery costs the lionesses their long manes forever.
summary.zh: 母獅讚猿之躍、大羚之疾、鴕鳥之吼；妒獅設宴，抓猿臀、劃羚面、拔鴕臀羽，揚長而去——然轉而獵鴕取肺，直至吼自胸膛。妻等始知供養者之貴；而一妻之譏笑，令母獅自此失其長鬣。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; contains domestic violence; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel II No. 37 (1920); not verbatim. The lions often come together in company, and then their wives always praise the apes for their nimbleness, the gemsbok for their speed, and the ostriches for their beautiful booming voice. This did not please the male lions at all, and they grew jealous about it and gave their dissatisfaction to their wives in full company; but the lionesses held that they were right.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The wives made a feast and dance and invited Ape, Gemsbok and Ostrich; the lionesses clapped hands and cheered Ape and Gemsbok and Ostrich, but not their own men. One lion scratched the hair off Ape's seat, another sprang on Gemsbok and scored marks in his face, the third stripped all the feathers off the Ostrich's rump; and the three males walked away and left their wives with the little children.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The lions went and hunted ostriches only to eat their lungs, so that they could boom as beautifully as the ostrich out of the forechest; and after they had eaten many ostrich lungs they no longer boomed as if they had tails in their mouths or bones in their throats. The wives sought their providers out again and promised to do better; and from then on, when Ostrich booms, they clap no more hands; but when their own men boom they feel grand and praise them, for it is harder than any other voice. Yet one wife began again to mock her man's mane; he grew so angry that he dragged her round by the head-hair and plucked her so bald that her head-hair never grew so long again; the other lionesses cut theirs off in fear — that is why their manes are not so long as the males' to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel II (1920), No. 37; not verbatim.
